o: Explain the steps and required conditions for comparing algorithms and consolidation.
Apply the algorithm or method to supplied data.
c: Searching locates a target; sorting rearranges values into a specified order.
Linear works on unsorted data; binary needs sorted data but often makes fewer comparisons for large lists.
Bubble swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs; insertion places the next key into a sorted prefix; merge divides and combines ordered sublists.
For examination questions, name the method, trace the data and justify any prerequisite or limitation.

m.title: Comparing Algorithms and Consolidation · worked example
m.q: A school stores an unsorted list of pupil IDs. Choose a suitable search, then explain what would change if the list were sorted. [5 marks]
st: Linear search works without sorting and checks entries in sequence.
If sorted, binary search could discard half of the active range after each comparison and generally need fewer checks for large lists. [5]

w: A sorted array contains 128 items. Which search is appropriate and why? [4]
Binary search [1] as sorting prerequisite is met [1]; midpoint comparisons halve the range [1], generally using fewer comparisons than linear search for large data [1].
A student says bubble and insertion sort are identical. Compare the two. [4]
Bubble compares/swaps neighbouring elements [1] over repeated passes [1]; insertion builds a sorted prefix [1] by shifting and inserting a key [1].
Explain the difference between searching for a value and sorting data. [3]
Search aims to locate a value/index [1]; sort reorders all items by a key [1]; binary search may require sorting first [1].

State the characteristic action of each sorting algorithm: bubble, insertion and merge. [3]

Source: Original OCR J277-style practice question.
Bubble: adjacent swaps [1]; insertion: insert key into sorted prefix [1]; merge: split then merge ordered sublists [1].

Explain why binary search may outperform linear search on a large sorted array. [4]

Source: Original OCR J277-style practice question.
Binary chooses midpoint [1] and discards half each unsuccessful check [1]; linear may inspect elements individually [1], so binary generally uses fewer checks for large sorted arrays [1].
